blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Backfires: The Court’s Revitalized ‘Substantial Evidence’ Standard
blogs.description: This post examines the Federal Circuit’s decision to grant a judgment as a matter of law (JMOL) of non‑infringement for the ’134 patent after a starkly contradictory expert. It unpacks the Fifth Circuit’s ‘substantial evidence’ standard for supporting a jury’s infringement verdict, contrasts it with the Fed. Cir.’s approach, and discusses how the case underscores the need for clarity and consistency in expert witness testimony in patent litigation.

blogs.title: Add ‘And’ to the Claim: How the Three‑Signal Amendment Re‑shaped Claim Scope
blogs.description: Explore how Finesse Wireless’s amendment from ‘two or three signals’ to ‘three signals’ in the ’775 patent touches on the gray area of claim scope and prosecution‑history estoppel. We delve into the court’s analysis of the semantics of ‘clear and unambiguous’ language, how a claim amendment can (or cannot) negate claim scope, and what the ruling signals for litigants when formulating or amending patent claims in the face of prior‑art challenges.

blogs.title: Inside the Frequency Maze: Internal vs. External PIM and the Anatomy of Interference Claims
blogs.description: This post demystifies the technical world of internal versus external intermodulation products (PIM) that underpin the ’134 and ’775 patents, and shows how the court interpreted the claim’s language about ‘signals of interest’ and ‘interference‑generating signals’. We’ll explore how the interplay of technical specifics and claim construction shaped the decision and what it teaches about drafting sound technical patents.

blogs.title: When Verdicts Snap: Why a $166 Million Damages Award Was Vacated After a JMOL Reversal
blogs.description: Take a deep dive into why the court vacated a massive lump‑sum damages award following the reversal of the infringement finding. We’ll trace the court’s analysis linking damages to the validity and infringement of the patents, discuss the procedural difference between a new trial on damages and a JMOL for damages, and consider the broader implications for future damages calculations in patent litigation.
